name: frozen
baseline: std::set, std::unordered_set (same constexpr perfect-hash design also backs frozen::unordered_map, the drop-in for std::unordered_map)
workload: Single-lookup microbenchmark of present/absent int and string keys in small (~dozens of keys) frozen containers vs. the equivalent std:: container.
claimed_speedup: frozen::unordered_set ~3.1x faster than std::unordered_set for present int keys (173 ns vs 544 ns), ~3.8x for absent keys (131 ns vs 500 ns); frozen::set ~2.6x faster than std::set for present int keys (58 ns vs 153 ns); string containers ~1.7x (set) to ~3.3x (unordered_set, absent key) faster (derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Containers are immutable/fixed-capacity: no insert/erase/rehash after construction (constexpr keys are permanently fixed; without constexpr, values may be updated but keys cannot). Compile time and template-instantiation cost grow with key-set size. Header-only, no runtime dependency.
caveats: Numbers are from a February 2018 Quarkslab blog post written by the library's own author, not from a benchmark artifact committed in the repo (the repo ships the bench source under benchmarks/ but no published results file). The cited numbers are for frozen::set/unordered_set vs std::set/std::unordered_set, not literally std::unordered_map, though frozen::unordered_map uses the same perfect-hash mechanism. Which standard-library implementation (libstdc++ vs libc++) Clang++-5.0 linked against is not stated. A second, earlier (2017) Quarkslab post comparing frozen to gperf and std::unordered_set on a dictionary-lookup task did not state compiler/hardware and measured wall-clock time that the author flagged as likely I/O-bound, so that post was not used as the primary source.
found_via: WebSearch: "frozen c++ header-only constexpr unordered_map benchmark speedup vs std::unordered_map" -> https://blog.quarkslab.com/frozen-zero-cost-initialization-for-immutable-containers-and-various-algorithms.html; repo found via gh search repos "gperf" language:C++

name: constexpr-phf (Kronuz/phf)
baseline: std::unordered_map, std::set, if-ladder, switch (binary search), gperf
workload: Integer-core find() at N=6..1000 keys; string dispatch benchmark hashing Xapiand's 192 field-type names, and a 570-word English stop-word filter over a 464K-word text, comparing hash-only and hash+verify constexpr-phf lookup against gperf, frozen::unordered_set, a compile-time trie, std::unordered_map and std::set.
claimed_speedup: vs unordered_map/if-ladder/switch: 1.2-1.3 ns/lookup for phf at N=6..1000 vs 2.4-162 ns (if-ladder), 4.0-40 ns (switch), 3.1-3.2 ns (unordered_map). String dispatch (192 field-type names): gperf 14 ns, phf hash-only 18 ns, phf hash+verify 21 ns, compile-time trie 28 ns, std::unordered_map 29 ns, frozen::unordered_set 40 ns, std::set 82 ns/op
tradeoffs: Integer keys only (strings must be pre-hashed by the caller, and hash-only lookups can misdispatch a non-member key unless verified). Fixed key set at build time, no insert/erase/rehash. Large key sets increase compile time since the perfect hash is searched at compile time.
caveats: First-party benchmark (project's own README/bench code); capped at C because hardware is stated only as "x86_64" with no CPU model, even though compiler and flags (GCC 11, -O3) are given. Numbers for gperf/frozen/trie come from the same repo's bench/ harness, not independently reproduced.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "gperf" language:C++ --sort stars

name: ConstexprCore/perfect_hash
baseline: std::unordered_map, gperf, frozen::unordered_map, absl::flat_hash_map, pthash, ankerl::unordered_dense, if/else chain
workload: Billion-queries-per-second table for the URL-protocol key set (http, https, ftp, ws, wss, file); a broader benchmark suite also covers S&P 100 tickers, C++ keywords, HTTP headers, MIME types, letters a-z, and JS reserved words, each queried hit-only/miss-only/mixed.
claimed_speedup: 1.08 billion queries/s for this library vs 0.23 (gperf), 0.22 (kronuz::phf), 0.16 (frozen::unordered_map), 0.14 (absl::flat_hash_map / pthash), 0.10 (std::unordered_map / ankerl::dense_hash_map), 0.19 (naive) -- roughly 10x std::unordered_map and 4x the next-fastest competitor
tradeoffs: Wide container needed past 255 keys or 254-byte keys (different code path, whole-key multiplicative hash). Requires C++23. Compile time grows with key-set size (raising -fconstexpr-steps/-fconstexpr-ops-limit is needed for large sets, e.g. ~5s for 5,581 keys).
caveats: No compiler name or optimization flags are stated for the headline billion-queries/s table (only "Apple M4 processor"), so it is capped at C despite the CPU model being named. The claimed 10x-over-unordered_map and 4x-over-next-competitor gap is large for a 6-key set; new project (first commit era unclear, 17 stars) so treat as an unverified first-party claim pending independent reproduction.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "gperf" language:C++ --sort stars; WebSearch: "gperf alternative constexpr perfect hash C++ faster than std::unordered_map github"

name: icy
workload: map/set find() and iteration for std::string_view and std::int64_t keys at N=16/512/1024, comparing icy::map/set (consteval-built, open-addressed) against std::map, std::unordered_map/set, tsl::robin_map/set, and a sorted-vector binary search.
claimed_speedup: std::string_view find() at N=1024: icy 3.228 cycles/op vs std::map 44.393, std::unordered_map 5.278, tsl::robin_map 4.595, sorted-vector+lb 23.987 (roughly 1.5-2x faster than std::unordered_map/set per the README's own summary, and up to ~14x faster than std::map, derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Best for small key sets; larger sets (>=1000) need -fconstexpr-steps tuning. Requires C++23 and consteval support. An ICY_OPTIMIZE_KEY_CMP macro skips key comparison in find() for extra speed at the cost of relying purely on hash equality.
caveats: Build config for the benchmark is RelWithDebInfo (not a bare -O3 Release build) and no compiler name/version or exact flags are given, so this is capped at C despite the CPU model being named. Brand-new project (0 stars, first commits recent), numbers are the author's own microbenchmark, not independently reproduced.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "compile time hash map" --sort stars

name: Flash Perfect Hash (fph-table)
baseline: std::unordered_map (also compared to absl::flat_hash_map, tsl::robin_map, ska::flat_hash_map, robin_hood::unordered_flat_map, emhash7 in the linked suite)
workload: find() (hit) on a 64-bit integer key hash table at max_load_factor=0.9, across dataset sizes, per the companion hashtable-bench suite's plots.
claimed_speedup: fph::DynamicFphMap shows a "clear speed advantage" for hit lookups on the tested integer dataset on both x86-64 and arm64 platforms (exact ns/op values are in the linked plots/CSVs, not reproduced as text in the README)
tradeoffs: Extremely fast lookup but slow insertion; whole table typically rebuilt on insert that breaks perfectness. Requires a seed-taking hash functor (SeedHash) unlike std::hash, or use of the MetaFph variant with a metadata array (extra memory, 2-8 bits/key overhead). Keys must be CopyConstructible, values MoveConstructible.
caveats: The linked hashtable-bench suite is maintained by the same author as fph-table, so it is not an independent third-party shootout despite testing many unrelated hash tables; capped at C. Exact compiler and flags for the AMD 3990x / Apple M1 Max plots are not stated in either README (only "Release" build type, GCC/Clang tested). The headline claim is qualitative ("clear speed advantage") rather than a quoted ns/op number in the fph-table README itself.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "CHD algorithm hash" / "fast lookup table generator" -> renzibei/fph-table

name: triehash
workload: Hash 1,000,000 times per word over the field names of Debian Packages/Sources files, measured in GB/s, across 7 machines/architectures (amd64, arm64, armel, armhf, ppc64el, mipsel).
claimed_speedup: On jak-x230 (amd64, Core i5-3320M): order-preserving Trie 2.4 GB/s vs gperf 1.3 GB/s (case-sensitive) / 0.7 GB/s (case-insensitive, "gperf (*)") -- roughly 1.8-3.4x faster than gperf depending on variant and architecture (derived from page data)
hardware: Mixed: "jak-x230" (stated elsewhere as Core i5-3320M), plus unnamed Debian porterbox machines for the other architectures
stars_or_usage: 49 stars; used in APT (Debian package manager)
tradeoffs: Order-preserving (unlike most minimal perfect hash schemes), which trades some construction flexibility for keeping key order in the output table. Generator only handles a fixed key set known at generation time (codegen tool, like gperf, not a runtime container).
caveats: Compiler (and its version/flags) is not stated for any of the measured machines, only listed as gcc-family via context; most machines beyond the x230 are named only by hostname, not CPU model, so hardware is only partially identified. It's a C code generator, not a C++ template library, but is directly callable from C++ (per the assignment's C-API rule).
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "gperf replacement C++" -> no hits; found via gh search repos "CHD algorithm hash" / follow-on search of gperf-family generators

name: cmph / cxxmph (mph_map)
workload: Lookup-heavy workload over large sets of URL keys (>100k) comparing cxxmph's mph_map/mph_set (BDZ-algorithm minimal perfect hash wrapped in an unordered_map-compatible interface) against std::unordered_map.
claimed_speedup: "about 10%-50% faster than unordered_map" for large (>100k) URL key sets with expensive comparisons (verbatim from the header comment)
tradeoffs: cxxmph containers are read-mostly: cheap lookups but the perfect hash is rebuilt on structural change, so it favors static/rarely-modified key sets. Author's own comment warns "those classes are not necessarily faster than their existing counterparts, benchmark your code before using it." Core cmph library targets very large (up to billions of) key sets, unlike gperf which targets small compile-time sets.
caveats: The 10-50% figure has no stated methodology at all (no benchmark code, compiler, flags, hardware, or dataset size beyond ">100k"), capping it at C. The GitHub mirror's last commit is from 2017 and the repo is effectively unmaintained; the underlying cmph project's canonical home is a SourceForge/Google Code-era release, so provenance of this mirror is secondary rather than primary.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "cxxmph" (found inside zvelo/cmph after zvelo/cmph surfaced via gh search repos "gperf" language:C++)
